title: Good Friday
hookLine: churches strip altars, keep silence, and venerate the cross

cards: On Good Friday, a church can look robbed. The altar is bare wood or stone. No flowers, no candles burning, the cloths gone.
Often the bells stay silent. People come in without talking, and sit. Some services start at noon and run until three in the afternoon.
Matthew writes: "Now from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land unto the ninth hour." By the old way of counting the day, that's noon to three.
So some Christians keep those hours, in silence, or with long readings, or a single hymn. Today's word is the day's strange name.

teach.b: Good Friday. First, what the Gospels say happened. After his arrest, Jesus is questioned by the high priest's council, then handed to Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor.
Pilate sentences him, and Roman soldiers crucify him outside the city wall. Crucifixion was a Roman punishment for rebels and slaves, meant to be slow and public. His friends mostly scatter.
Women who had followed him from Galilee stay, watching. In John's Gospel, his last words are three in English: "It is finished."
In Greek, a single word: tetelestai. Not it's over, I give up, but complete, done, accomplished. Christians hear it as the end of a work, not a defeat.
So why call the day good?
Honestly, nobody is sure. Good may be the old English sense of holy; some suggest it came from God's Friday. The sources don't settle it.
But Christians call it good because they believe something was done that day for the whole world, out of love, and they explain how in more than one way. Churches keep the day differently.

teach.h: THE CROSS, THE TOMB, THE DARK.
teach.b: Catholics celebrate no Mass; in the afternoon they read the Passion, and people come forward one by one to kneel before the cross, touch it, or kiss it.
Orthodox Christians carry a cloth icon of Christ's burial in procession and lay it in a tomb decked with flowers.
Some Protestants gather for three hours at noon, or for a service where candles are put out one by one, until the church is dark.

how: On Good Friday churches are left bare and some Christians fast and keep silence; Catholics venerate the cross at an afternoon service without Mass, Orthodox Christians carry the epitaphios, an icon of Christ's burial, in procession, and some Protestants keep services from noon to three.

games.q: you're one of the women who followed Jesus from Galilee. he's on a Roman cross, and most of his friends have run. what do you do?
o: stay, and watch, and don't leave.
go and argue with the soldiers.
games.why: the Gospels say women who had followed him stayed and watched. they're the ones who see where he is buried.

practice: For the next two minutes, keep silence: no music, no plans, no words. If you have a cross, you can look at it.
If you pray, simply stay near it, the way the women stayed; if you don't, let the silence be for anyone who is suffering today.

wordCard.voice: Good Friday. The day Christians remember Jesus's death on the cross, with bare altars, silence and the veneration of the cross. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: it is finished, completed, accomplished. one word in John 19:30.

carryVoice: Your line: it is finished. Not over, but complete: the end of a work. That's day one hundred seventeen.
